query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys, increasing the concentration of HCP-forming elements and adding a minor amount of boron leads to a dual mechanistic effect: (1) the higher HCP content enhances lattice distortions and reduces dislocation core energies, thereby altering slip-system activation and improving ductility, and (2) boron addition precipitates intergranular HCP borides that improve grain boundary cohesion and thermoelastic response.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., one with primarily BCC elements such as VNbMoTaW) without significant HCP elements or boron addition.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by increasing the fraction of HCP-forming elements (e.g., Ti, Zr, Hf) and by adding a minor amount (~0.1 at.%) of boron.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under controlled temperatures ranging from room temperature to elevated temperatures (300 °C–800 °C) under both quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions; appropriate heat treatment conditions to ensure solid-solution and grain-boundary phase development.
generation.structural_mediator: Altered dislocation core structure and lattice distortion due to increased HCP element concentration, and the formation of HCP boride precipitates at grain boundaries from boron addition.
generation.mechanism: The increased HCP element content reduces the dislocation core energy and changes the active slip planes (due to enhanced lattice distortion), which improves plasticity and thermoelastic performance. Concurrently, the boron-induced precipitation of HCP borides at grain boundaries enhances intergranular cohesion, reducing the propensity for intergranular fracture and promoting transgranular failure that retards crack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy is expected to display lower brittle-to-ductile transition temperature, higher work hardenability, and a shift from intergranular to transgranular fracture modes, along with altered slip behavior (e.g., activation of additional {110} slip planes).
generation.baseline: The original RHEA with primarily BCC elements without additional HCP-forming elements or boron, exhibiting higher dislocation core energy, less lattice distortion, and pronounced intergranular fracture under high-temperature stress.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature service conditions typical for refractory alloys (300 °C–800 °C) and for alloys processed to achieve a homogeneous BCC solid-solution matrix; effects might be limited if the volume fraction of HCP phases or boride precipitation is too low to impact macroscopic mechanical behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in ductility and thermoelastic response (e.g., precise changes in critical resolved shear stresses and fracture toughness) are uncertain and require detailed experimental characterization. Variations in processing parameters may also influence the degree of HCP phase precipitation and dislocation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline BCC composition and one with increased HCP element content plus 0.1 at.% boron addition. Subject both sets to identical thermo-mechanical testing regimes including high-temperature creep, nanoindentation, and fracture mode analysis using electron microscopy. Compare dislocation slip patterns and grain boundary fracture mechanisms.
measurements: Nanoindentation hardness and modulus to assess changes in elastic-plastic response
Tensile and creep tests at temperatures between 300 °C and 800 °C to determine ductility and work hardenability
Microscopic evaluation (e.g., SEM/TEM) of dislocation structures and fracture surfaces to identify slip systems and fracture modes
X-ray diffraction and/or electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to quantify phase distributions (BCC matrix versus HCP boride precipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant shift towards transgranular fracture, reduced brittle-to-ductile transition temperature, enhanced work hardening, or altered slip system activation compared to the baseline alloy under identical testing conditions, then the dual mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a new class of alloys that consist of more than four alloying elements in close to equiatomic concentrations (). The diverse compositional possibilities of HEAs, combined with appropriate heat treatment conditions, offer the potential to develop new alloys with a combination of remarkable properties such as outstanding mechanical properties, high-hydrogen absorption capacity, and robust resistance to corrosion and radiation (). The refractory HEAs (RHEAs) based on refractory elements were proposed by Senkov et al. () as a new class of high-temperature structural alloys that might surpass the capabilities of nickel-based superalloys. RHEAs are emerging as prominent contenders in diverse industries, notably in the nuclear and aerospace sectors (, ).

AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. Our findings demonstrate how ductility and strength can be controlled through the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in RHEAs.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties Poor ductility is a major drawback of otherwise promising refractory

Based on the above results, we hypothesized that the higher concentration of HCP elements in TiZrNbHfTa than in VNbMoTaW is what causes a significant change in lattice distortion, dislocation core structure, and slip behavior and that the same may be the case in other BCC RHEAs. AbstractIn order to find more excellent structural materials resistant to radiation damage, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been developed due to their characteristics of limited point defect diffusion such as lattice distortion and slow diffusion. Specially, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) that can adapt to a high-temperature environment are badly needed. In this study, TiZrHfNbMo0.1 RHEAs are selected for irradiation and nanoindentation experiments. We combined the mechanistic model for the depth-dependent hardness of ion-irradiated metals and the introduction of the scale factor f to modify the irradiation-hardening model in order to better describe the nanoindentation indentation process in the irradiated layer. Finally, it can be found that, with the increase in irradiation dose, a more serious lattice distortion caused by a higher defect density limits the expansion of the plastic zone.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical properties, ion irradiation, indentation size effect, plastic zone

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.

chosen.approach: Element composition modifications (HCP elements, boron) in RHEAs
